claim: Recent studies suggest that cells make stochastic choices with respect to differentiation or division.
source: Recent studies suggest that cells make stochastic choices with respect to differentiation or division.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation from recent studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: The timing of vertebrate neuronal differentiation is regulated by molecular oscillations of HES1, tuned by miR-9.
source: We previously proposed that the timing of vertebrate neuronal differentiation is regulated by molecular oscillations of a transcriptional repressor, HES1, tuned by a post-transcriptional repressor, miR-9.
evidence: This is a previously proposed model by the authors, referenced in the abstract.

claim: Increased stochasticity spreads the timing of differentiation in a population.
source: We report that increased stochasticity spreads the timing of differentiation in a population, such that initially equivalent cells differentiate over a period of time.
evidence: This is a main finding reported in the abstract based on computational modeling.

claim: Inherent stochasticity increases the robustness of the progenitor state.
source: Surprisingly, inherent stochasticity also increases the robustness of the progenitor state and lessens the impact of unequal, random distribution of molecules at cell division on the temporal spread of differentiation at the population level.
evidence: This is a key finding from the computational modeling presented in the study.

claim: The nervous system contains many different cell types generated by actively dividing progenitor cells in a sequential order during embryogenesis.
source: The nervous system is a complex organ system with many different cell types. These are generated by actively dividing progenitor cells in a sequential order during embryogenesis, while progenitor cells themselves change their character along the way (Götz and Huttner, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Götz and Huttner, 2005.

claim: In the mammalian cortex and vertebrate retina, certain cell types are generated early while others are generated late.
source: In cases where histogenesis of neural tissues has been examined, such as the mammalian cortex and the vertebrate retina, a temporal order has been found such that certain cell types are generated early while others are generated late (Franco et al., 2012; Bertrand et al., 2002; Boije et al., 2014; Greig et al., 2013; Franco and Müller, 2013; Goetz et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2006; Gaspard et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Recent experiments based on single-cell lineage mapping in the zebrafish retina have shown that the timing of differentiation can be a fundamentally stochastic process.
source: Therefore, it was surprising that recent experiments based on single-cell lineage mapping in the zebrafish retina have shown that the timing of differentiation can be a fundamentally stochastic process, although the collective behaviour of many progenitors forms a reproducible retina (He et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2012.

claim: Rat retinal progenitor cells cultured at single-cell density and constant extracellular environment show stochastic differentiation timing.
source: A similar conclusion was reached in a study where rat retinal progenitor cells were cultured at single-cell density and constant extracellular environment (Gomes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomes et al., 2011.

claim: Hes genes, including Hes1 and Hes5, regulate the balance between differentiation and maintenance of progenitors in the developing nervous system.
source: At a molecular level, the balance between differentiation and the maintenance of progenitors in the developing nervous system is regulated by transcriptional repressors such as the Hes gene family, including Hes1 and Hes5 (Kageyama et al., 2007, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kageyama et al., 2007, 2008.

claim: When Hes genes are absent, neural progenitors prematurely differentiate and cause defects in brain formation.
source: When Hes genes are absent, neural progenitors prematurely differentiate and cause a wide range of defects in brain formation (Hatakeyama et al., 2004; Nakamura et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hatakeyama et al., 2004 and Nakamura et al., 2000.

claim: Overexpression of Hes genes leads to inhibition of neurogenesis and over-maintenance of neural progenitors.
source: Conversely, overexpression of Hes genes leads to inhibition of neurogenesis and over-maintenance of neural progenitors (Ishibashi et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishibashi et al., 1995.

claim: Hes1 is expressed in an oscillatory manner with a period of around 2 hr in neural progenitors.
source: Hes1 is expressed in an oscillatory manner with a period of around 2 hr in neural progenitors (Imayoshi et al., 2013; Shimojo et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Imayoshi et al., 2013 and Shimojo et al., 2008.

claim: Hes1 is expressed at a low steady state in differentiated neurons.
source: but is expressed at a low steady state in differentiated neurons (Imayoshi et al., 2013; Sasai et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Imayoshi et al., 2013 and Sasai et al., 1992.

claim: Light-induced oscillatory expression of Ascl1 increased the proportion of dividing cells in Ascl1-null neural progenitors.
source: It was shown that light-induced oscillatory expression of Ascl1 increased the proportion of dividing cells in Ascl1-null neural progenitors, whereas sustained Ascl1 expression increased the efficiency of neuronal differentiation (Imayoshi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imayoshi et al., 2013.

claim: Light-induced sustained expression of Dll1 leads to higher levels of p21 than oscillatory expression.
source: It has similarly been shown that light-induced sustained expression of the Delta ligand Dll1 leads to higher levels of the cell cycle inhibitor p21 than oscillatory expression (Shimojo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shimojo et al., 2016.

claim: Hes1 oscillates in neural progenitors due to a combination of delayed negative self-repression and relatively fast degradation of Hes1 mRNA and HES1 protein.
source: Experimental and theoretical work has shown that Hes1 oscillates in neural progenitors possibly due to a combination of delayed negative self-repression and relatively fast degradation of Hes1 mRNA and HES1 protein, previously measured in fibroblasts (Jensen et al., 2003; Monk, 2003; Hirata et al., 2002; Momiji and Monk, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2003; Monk, 2003; Hirata et al., 2002; Momiji and Monk, 2008.

claim: Hes1 is a primary target of the microRNA miR-9.
source: Recent experimental results have shown that Hes1 is a primary target of the microRNA miR-9, and HES1 also periodically represses the transcription of miR-9, thus forming a double negative feedback loop (Bonev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bonev et al., 2012.

claim: Mature miR-9 is very stable and accumulates over time in a gradual manner.
source: However, mature miR-9 is very stable and accumulates over time in a gradual manner.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Accumulating levels of miR-9 beyond a certain level can cause oscillations of Hes1 to cease, leading to differentiation.
source: It has been proposed that accumulating levels of miR-9 beyond a certain level can cause oscillations of Hes1 to cease, leading to differentiation (Bonev et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonev et al., 2012 and Tan et al., 2012.

claim: The Hes1/miR-9 interaction has been mathematically modelled using deterministic delay differential equations.
source: The Hes1/miR-9 interaction has been mathematically modelled using deterministic delay differential equations (Goodfellow et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodfellow et al., 2014.

claim: Interactions within the Hes1/miR-9 network can lead to the emergence of bistability and Hopf bifurcations.
source: This showed that interactions within the Hes1/miR-9 network can lead to the emergence of bistability (alternative cell fates) and Hopf bifurcations (separating stable states from an oscillatory regime).
evidence: This is a result from the deterministic modeling study by Goodfellow et al., 2014.

claim: High cell-to-cell variability exists in the abundance of Hes1 mRNA and protein in undifferentiated neural cells.
source: Here, we show that high cell-to-cell variability exists in the abundance of Hes1 mRNA and protein in undifferentiated neural cells (progenitor and stem cells) as evidenced by quantitative single-molecule Fluorescent in Situ Hybridisation (smFISH) and Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy (FCS), respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work in this study.

claim: The copy number of Hes1 mRNA, protein and miR-9 per cell is low.
source: Furthermore, the copy number of Hes1 mRNA, protein and miR-9 per cell is low, (determined by smFISH, FCS and stem loop qRT-PCR, respectively)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work in this study using multiple quantitative methods.

claim: In C17.2 neural progenitor cells, an average of 72 copies of Hes1 mRNA per cell was detected by smFISH.
source: In C17.2 neural progenitor cells, we detected an average of 72 copies Hes1 mRNA/cell by smFISH (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from smFISH experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In C17.2 neural progenitor cells, an average of 88 copies of Hes1 mRNA per cell was detected by qRT-PCR.
source: and an average of 88 copies by qRT-PCR (data not shown), confirming the result.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from qRT-PCR experiments that confirms the smFISH result.

claim: In Tau-GFP NS cells grown under proliferative conditions, the average was only 11 copies of Hes1 mRNA per cell by smFISH.
source: In Tau-GFP NS cells grown under proliferative conditions (GFP negative cells; Figure 1D and E), the average was only 11 copies of Hes1 mRNA/cell by smFISH.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from smFISH experiments shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Spontaneously differentiated cells identified by high-intensity GFP expression were mostly negative for Hes1 mRNA transcript.
source: A few spontaneously differentiated cells, identified by high-intensity GFP expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), were mostly negative for Hes1 mRNA transcript, indicating that the gene is switched off upon differentiation (average 0.8 copies per cell) (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is a finding from smFISH experiments shown in Figure 1D, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mature miR-9 was present in an average copy number of 1100 ± 20 (S.E.M) molecules per cell in C17.2 cells.
source: Mature miR-9 was present in an average copy number of 1100 ± 20 (S.E.M) molecules per cell, significantly lower than other reported microRNAs and surprisingly low considering the hundreds of miR-9 targets (Bonev et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from stem-loop Taqman qRT-PCR shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: FCS quantification gave an estimate of 3660 ± 120 (S.E.M) molecules of VENUS:HES1 per nucleus when driven by the UbC promoter.
source: This gave an estimate of 3660 ± 120 (S.E.M) molecules of VENUS:HES1 per nucleus when driven by the UbC promoter (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FCS experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average abundance of endogenous HES1 is approximately 2930 molecules per nucleus.
source: This suggests an average abundance of endogenous HES1 of 2930 molecules per nucleus which is significantly lower than the median protein abundance of 50,000 copies per cell previously reported from global quantification studies (Schwanhausser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is calculated from FCS measurements and western blot ratios, compared to literature values from Schwanhausser et al., 2011.

claim: FCS quantification of VENUS:HES1 driven by the Hes1 promoter gave 2450 ± 190 (S.E.M) molecules per nucleus.
source: Furthermore, FCS quantification of VENUS:HES1 driven by the Hes1 promoter gave a similar value, that is 2450 ± 190 (S.E.M) molecules per nucleus (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FCS experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The stochastic simulation matches the experimental data better than the deterministic simulation, both at the single-cell and the population level.
source: Thus, the stochastic simulation matches the experimental data better, both at the single-cell and the population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulations with experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In deterministic simulations, all cells that start with the same parameters and conditions differentiate at the same time.
source: In deterministic simulations, all cells that start with the same parameters and conditions differentiate at the same time.
evidence: This is a property of deterministic models.

claim: At high system size (Ω=50), the distribution of times to reach the low HES1 state is narrow.
source: The time taken to reach the low HES1 protein threshold was calculated for 2000 simulations using the dSSA, and the distribution of times to reach the low HES1 state is narrow for Ω=50 (Figure 4B), approaching the deterministic solution.
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: As the system size decreases, the distribution in the timing of differentiation becomes increasingly broad.
source: At the same time, the distribution in the timing of differentiation of 2000 independent simulations becomes increasingly broad as the system size decreases (Figures 4E and H).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic simulations shown in Figures 4E and H.

claim: The average of the distribution of differentiation timing becomes gradually shifted towards earlier times as system size is reduced.
source: When we reduced the system size we unexpectedly found that the average of the distribution also became gradually shifted towards earlier times (e.g. compare Figure 4B with Figure 4E and H, where scaling of mean with system size shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic simulations shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing the amount of miR-9 brought forward and reduced the spread of time to differentiation events in a simulated population.
source: In the stochastic model increasing the amount of miR-9 brought forward and reduced the spread of time to differentiation events in a simulated population (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic simulations shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Increasing miR-9 in C17.2 neural progenitor cells increased the number of Tuj1-positive neurons earlier than in control cultures.
source: Increasing miR-9 in C17.2 neural progenitor cells increased the number of Tuj1-positive neurons earlier than in control cultures after several days, without affecting the total cell number (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transfecting C17.2 cells with control mimic showed a broad spread in the timing of differentiation (standard deviation = 48 hr).
source: Transfecting the C17.2 cells with a control mimic and measuring the number of Tuj1-positive neuronal cells showed a broad spread in the timing of differentiation (standard deviation = 48 hr, Figure 6D)
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When cells were transfected with 50 nM or 100 nM of miR-9 mimic the average time to differentiation decreased and the spread became narrower.
source: When cells were transfected with 50 nM or 100 nM of miR-9 mimic the average time to differentiation decreased and the spread became narrower in a miR-9 initial concentration dependent way (standard deviation = 24 hr and 17 hr respectively, Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Stochasticity has made the oscillatory state more robust to an increase in miR-9.
source: We propose that stochasticity has made the oscillatory state more robust to an increase in miR-9 in the sense that the stochastic HES1 oscillator continues to operate under conditions (i.e. parameter values) where the deterministic equivalent will have stopped.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing deterministic and stochastic models in parameter space.

claim: Very few NS cell divisions partitioned Hes1 mRNA equally and some showed a highly asymmetric distribution.
source: Very few of these divisions partitioned Hes1 mRNA equally and some showed a highly asymmetric distribution (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from smFISH shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: The majority of cell divisions (36/51) were mostly consistent with a binomial mode of division.
source: The majority of cell divisions (36/51) were mostly consistent with a binomial mode of division (p-value>0.05, binomial distribution with Bonferroni multiple testing adjusted p-value), with a few outliers.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the smFISH data on Hes1 mRNA partitioning at cell division.

claim: The stochastic system is more robust than the deterministic system to noise introduced at cell division.
source: We conclude that the stochastic system is more robust than the deterministic system to noise introduced at cell division because it produces the same distribution of differentiation at the population level irrespective of whether the cells distribute molecules randomly or equally at cell division, at all system sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulations with different modes of division shown in Figure 9.

claim: The activity of miR-9 increases specifically in neuronally differentiated cells.
source: Here, using a miR-9 sensor we show that the activity of miR-9 increases specifically in neuronally differentiated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding using a miR-9 sensor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intronic probe for Hes1 showed transcription in GFP negative cells but no transcription in GFP positive neuronally differentiated cells.
source: This was confirmed by using an intronic probe for Hes1 which showed transcription in GFP negative cells (Figure 1H, corresponding exonic shown in G, I) but no transcription in GFP positive neuronally differentiated cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from smFISH shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: Single-cell luciferase imaging of primary NS cells containing a LUC2:HES1 fusion BAC reporter shows a high degree of noise evident as peak-to-peak variability in amplitude and period.
source: Single-cell luciferase imaging of primary NS cells containing a Luciferase2-HES1 (LUC2:HES1) fusion BAC reporter (Imayoshi et al., 2013) shows a high degree of noise evident as peak-to-peak variability in amplitude and period.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: At the population level, oscillations in Hes1 mRNA quickly dampen in serum synchronised C17.2 cells.
source: At the population level, analysed by qRT-PCR of serum synchronised C17.2 cells, oscillations in Hes1 mRNA quickly dampen, presumably because cells drift out of synchrony (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The average expression of a population of 2000 stochastic simulations shows faster dampening than deterministic simulations.
source: The average expression of a population of 2000 stochastic simulations using the dSSA shows faster dampening (Figure 3F) than deterministic simulations (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing stochastic and deterministic simulations shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The long-tail distribution of mRNA molecules in NS cells may be indicative of slow switching between transcriptionally active and inactive promoter states.
source: The long-tail distribution of mRNA molecules in NS cells may be indicative of slow switching between transcriptionally active and inactive promoter states (Munsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data with reference to Munsky et al., 2012.

claim: The Hes1 mRNA copy number is close to the reported global median of 17 copies per cell.
source: In particular, while the Hes1 mRNA copy number is close to the reported global median of 17 copies per cell, the HES1 protein abundance is well below the median value of 50,000 copies per cell (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured Hes1 mRNA copy number to literature values from Schwanhäusser et al., 2011.

claim: The average measured miR-9 copy number (1100 copies) in C17.2 cells is on the low side of the previously reported range of 10 to more than 30,000 copies per cell.
source: The average measured miR-9 copy number (1100 copies) in C17.2 cells is also on the low side of the previously reported range of 10 to more than 30,000 copies per cell (Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured miR-9 copy number to literature values from Chen et al., 2005.

claim: The abundance of HES1 protein and miR-9 is low considering the number of their predicted molecular targets.
source: We consider the abundance of HES1 protein and miR-9 to be low not only compared to average global abundancies, but also considering the number of their predicted molecular targets (3,074 for HES1, (Margolin et al., 2009); and more than 500 for miR-9, (Bonev et al., 2011)).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured abundances in the context of the number of targets, with citations to Margolin et al., 2009 and Bonev et al., 2011.

claim: Randomness originating in the finite copy number within transcriptional programmes provides a theoretical framework to understand the heterogeneity observed in single-cell time series of neural stem cells.
source: Together, our work demonstrates that randomness originating in the finite copy number within transcriptional programmes provides a theoretical framework to understand the heterogeneity observed in single-cell time series of neural stem (NS) cells and its consequences for neural development.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study integrating computational and experimental findings.

claim: Developing systems may exploit stochasticity in gene regulatory networks to stagger differentiation time, cope with noise introduced by unequal inheritance of components and safeguard the progenitor state.
source: Developing systems may exploit stochasticity in gene regulatory networks to stagger differentiation time, cope with noise introduced by unequal inheritance of components and safeguard the progenitor state.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the computational and experimental findings.

claim: A distribution in timing of differentiation is not only linked to the generation of different cell types, but also occurs when considering the generation of a single particular cell type.
source: However, a distribution in timing of differentiation is not only linked to the generation of different cell types, because when one considers the generation of a single particular cell type, there is again a distribution in the timing of birth of this cell type (Gaspard et al., 2008; Gomes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gaspard et al., 2008 and Gomes et al., 2011.

claim: The spread of the timing distribution is inversely related to the absolute number of interacting molecules.
source: However, in the stochastic framework the time-to-differentiation of such cells becomes distributed, with the spread of the distribution inversely related to the absolute number of interacting molecules.
evidence: This is a finding from the stochastic modeling shown in Figure 4.

claim: Due to the ability of intrinsic noise to induce oscillatory dynamics, Hes1 oscillations are maintained for a greater range of parameters than in the deterministic system.
source: Due to the ability of intrinsic noise to induce oscillatory dynamics, Hes1 oscillations are maintained for a greater range of parameters than in the deterministic system, which can be interpreted as increased robustness of the progenitor state in the stochastic model.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing deterministic and stochastic models in parameter space shown in Figure 7.

claim: The average time of differentiation can be shifted by varying the molecular copy number or by varying the initial miR-9 levels.
source: Computationally, the average time of differentiation can be shifted by varying the molecular copy number or by varying the initial miR-9 levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: The stochastic network is able to better 'absorb' noise attributable to unequal distribution of some molecular components at division.
source: Finally, we show that the stochastic network is able to better 'absorb' noise attributable to unequal distribution of some molecular components at division, maintaining its output as if the divisions were symmetric and thus giving a robust outcome at a population level.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 9.

claim: The number of interacting molecules within a cell is an important parameter that can be tuned to control the onset of differentiation.
source: This supports the idea that the number of interacting molecules within a cell is an important parameter that can be tuned to control the onset of differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: It may be advantageous for differentiation events to have a broad distribution, as this could be used to generate cell-type diversity, if coupled with mechanisms of cell-type specification.
source: We suggest that it may be advantageous for differentiation events to have a broad distribution, as this could be used to generate cell-type diversity, if coupled with mechanisms of cell-type specification (Qian et al., 2000; Temple, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results, with citations to Qian et al., 2000 and Temple, 2001.

claim: A distribution in the timing of differentiation is a widespread property, which is perhaps advantageous in allowing a time window for feedback control such that the right cell numbers are produced.
source: This suggests that a distribution in the timing of differentiation is a widespread property, which is perhaps advantageous in allowing a time window for feedback control such that the right cell numbers are produced.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that timing distributions occur in multiple contexts.

claim: There is a continuum of behaviours since the spread of the timing distribution is a function of the system size.
source: Our modelling also showed that there is a continuum of behaviours since the spread of the timing distribution is a function of the system size, where high system size gives rise to a narrow distribution and low system size to a broad distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the stochastic modeling shown in Figure 4.

claim: The low molecular copy number is not an exclusive source of cell-to-cell heterogeneity.
source: However, the low molecular copy number is not an exclusive source of cell-to-cell heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging other potential sources of heterogeneity.

claim: The Hes1 gene is also involved in the Notch signalling pathway of cell-cell communication.
source: The Hes1 gene is also involved in the Notch signalling pathway of cell-cell communication, and other studies have considered the effect of noise in the Notch pathway (Jenkins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jenkins et al., 2015.

claim: In the promoter ON/OFF model, periods of gene activity are interspersed by transcriptional silence, leading to bursty behaviour.
source: In the promoter ON/OFF model, periods of gene activity are interspersed by transcriptional silence, leading to bursty behaviour (Suter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suter et al., 2011.

claim: Bursting models of transcription have been shown to fit the statistics of mRNA distributions measured by smFISH in multiple different systems.
source: Bursting models of transcription have been shown to fit the statistics of mRNA distributions measured by smFISH in multiple different systems (Munsky et al., 2012; Neuert et al., 2013; Bahar Halpern et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Munsky et al., 2012; Neuert et al., 2013; Bahar Halpern et al., 2015.

claim: Bursting models have also been fitted to live time series of transcription.
source: and have also been fitted to live time series of transcription (Harper et al., 2011; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014; Zechner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harper et al., 2011; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014; Zechner et al., 2014.

claim: Previous studies in bacteria have shown that partitioning is approximately binomial.
source: Previous studies in bacteria have also shown that partitioning is approximately binomial (Golding et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Golding et al., 2005.

claim: A binomial distribution would be expected if each mRNA molecule is partitioned independently into the two daughter cells and where the probability of inheriting an mRNA is equal to the ratio of the cell areas of the daughter cells.
source: A binomial distribution would be expected if each mRNA molecule is partitioned independently into the two daughter cells and where the probability of inheriting an mRNA is equal to the ratio of the cell areas of the daughter cells.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on statistical principles.
